title: Container Administration Command
summary: Container administration command abuse means using the management interface of a container platform to run code inside a container instead of on the host. The Docker daemon, the Kubernetes API server, and the kubelet all expose APIs that legitimately allow remote management, and anyone who obtains suitable credentials, a service account token, or reachability to an unauthenticated socket can turn those APIs into an execution channel. Documented mechanisms include specifying a command or entrypoint override when a container is started, attaching to an already running container with an exec style call, or talking to the API directly over its network port. On a host, the Docker socket is a frequent find, because writing to it is effectively root equivalent. Detection centres on platform audit logs recording exec and create requests, on process trees inside containers that do not match the image's normal behaviour, and on administrative clients invoked from hosts that never normally manage the platform.

beginner.definition: Containers are small packaged environments that run one application each. A container administration service is the tool that starts and controls those containers. An attacker who reaches that service can ask it to run commands for them inside a container. This gives them a foothold on your systems.
beginner.whyItMatters: The management service is powerful by design, so it rarely needs a bug to be useful to an attacker. One stolen key or one exposed port can turn it into a remote command channel. Commands then run with the container's permissions, which are often wider than people expect. If you never review the audit log, this activity leaves no trace on your radar.
howItWorks: The attacker finds a container platform, such as Docker or Kubernetes, on the network.
They look for an open management port or an unprotected socket file on a host.
With access, they ask the service to start a container with a command of their choice.
Alternatively they attach to a container already running and open a shell inside it.
The command runs with the permissions the container was given, which may be broad.
Logs from the management service record the request and the account that made it.
beginner.example: Think of an office building with a maintenance key cabinet at the front desk. Staff use it every day to enter plant rooms and fix things, and the cabinet is meant for the building team only. If a visitor reaches it and takes a key, they can walk into any plant room and work on equipment as if they belonged there. Nothing looks broken. The only clue is the logbook, which shows a key taken when no maintenance was scheduled.
takeaways: Container management services are execution channels, not just admin tools.
An exposed socket or a stolen token is often enough, with no software flaw needed.
Audit logs of exec and create requests are your main evidence.

objectives: Explain how a container administration service can be used to run commands.
Distinguish between starting a container with a chosen command and attaching to a running one.
Identify the permissions and interfaces that make this technique powerful.
Describe which platform audit log entries reveal this activity.
Explain why host access to a container management socket is high risk.
